1156.title: The four books of the Shia
1156.word: The four books of the Shia
1156.hook: al-Kafi, Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, Tahdhib and Istibsar, with their own science of grading
1156.howItsDone: Twelver Shia scholars study the four books with teachers, and a jurist weighs each report's chain and grade before relying on it in a ruling.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Malik and Ahmad, the Muwatta of Medina and the Musnad, arranged by Companion.

For the one who has no jurist at hand. That's the title of a book, put into English: Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih. Tradition says its author wrote it for people who had no scholar nearby to ask, so they could still find what they needed. It's one of a set of four. Shia Muslims also gathered the reports they trusted, through their own chains, checked by their own scholars. Today, their shelf. The four books of the Shia.
screen: `NO JURIST AT HAND.` → `ONE OF A SET OF FOUR.` → `ANOTHER SHELF.`

segments.voice: First, the names. Al-Kafi, the sufficient, compiled by al-Kulayni. Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, by the scholar known as Shaykh al-Saduq. And two by Shaykh al-Tusi: Tahdhib al-Ahkam, the refining of the rulings, and al-Istibsar, a close look at reports that seem to disagree with each other. Four books, three compilers. Second, what's inside. These books carry reports of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and also reports from the Imams of his family, beginning with Ali, whom Twelver Shia Muslims follow as the rightful guides after the Prophet. For Shia Muslims, the Imams are a trusted channel for the Prophet's teaching, so a chain may run through Ja'far al-Sadiq, or his father, back to the Prophet himself. Third, a beginning. Al-Kafi doesn't open with purity or prayer. Its first book is the book of intellect and ignorance: reports about reason, what it's worth, and what it's for. A collection of religion that starts with the mind. Fourth, the grading. Shia scholars have debated how far a report can rest on the book it sits in. Some, known as the Akhbaris, trusted the four books' reports broadly. Others hold that no book is sound cover to cover by its name alone: with their own science of narrators and their own grades, they weigh each report one at a time. Later scholars wrote commentaries that walk through al-Kafi report by report, judging each chain. So the habit of asking who told whom runs here too, along its own roads. Sunni and Shia Muslims keep different shelves. Today is about this one, on its own terms.
screen: `FOUR BOOKS, THREE COMPILERS.` · `THE PROPHET, AND THE IMAMS OF HIS FAMILY.` · `AL-KAFI OPENS WITH THE INTELLECT.` · `EACH REPORT WEIGHED ON ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Say each name with its meaning: al-Kafi, the sufficient; Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, for the one with no jurist at hand; Tahdhib al-Ahkam, the refining of the rulings; al-Istibsar, a close look at reports that seem to disagree. Then say only the four names, and see if the meanings come back. Last, sit with where the first one begins, a book of faith that opens with the mind, and name to yourself one question you've been avoiding thinking through, without trying to solve it.
The four books of the Shia. Al-Kafi, Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, Tahdhib al-Ahkam and al-Istibsar, each report in them weighed by its own chain. Today's word.

1157.title: Sacred hadith
1157.hook: words from Allah in the Prophet's phrasing, not part of the Qur'an
1157.tomorrow: I am as My servant thinks
1157.howItsDone: Muslims read hadith qudsi for reflection and teaching, and some books gather them in one place; they are not recited as Qur'an in the ritual prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four books of the Shia, a shelf that opens with the mind.

O My servants. A report in Sahih Muslim opens with those words, and the voice speaking isn't the Prophet's own. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is relating what Allah said: O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an. You won't find it in any surah. And yet the one speaking, in the first person, is Allah. So what kind of text is this? Today's word: hadith qudsi.
screen: `O MY SERVANTS.` → `NOT A VERSE OF THE QUR'AN.` → `SO WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Hadith, a report. Qudsi, holy. So: a sacred report, one in which the Prophet relates words from Allah. Second, the layers. The Prophet said that Allah said. One voice carried inside another, like a letter read aloud by the person who received it. That's today's line: allah said, he said. Third, how it differs from the Qur'an. Scholars explain it this way. The Qur'an is Allah's word in its meaning and its wording, recited in prayer, its very sound counted as revelation. A hadith qudsi carries meaning from Allah, in the Prophet's own phrasing. It isn't recited as Qur'an in the prayer. And it's graded like any other hadith, by its chain, so some are sound and some are weak. Everything from the last two weeks still applies. Fourth, the tone: it comes close. The report from Muslim keeps going. O My servants, all of you are hungry except the one I feed, so ask Me for food and I will feed you. All of you are unclothed except the one I clothe, so ask Me for clothing. And near its end: if every one of you, first and last, asked, and each were given what they asked, it would take from what Allah has no more than a needle takes from the sea when it's dipped in and lifted out. A voice that speaks of hunger, clothes, mistakes and asking. Not distant at all.
screen: `QUDSI: HOLY, SACRED.` · `THE PROPHET SAID THAT ALLAH SAID.` · `MEANING FROM ALLAH, THE PROPHET'S WORDS.` · `A NEEDLE DIPPED IN THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Read it a line at a time, with a breath between each: I have forbidden injustice for Myself; and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another; ask Me for food, and I will feed you; a needle, dipped in the sea. Then think of someone you might wrong without meaning to, by a word, a delay, a shortcut, and just see their face. If you pray, you can carry the line about asking into your next prayer.
Hadith qudsi. A sacred report: words from Allah that the Prophet relates in his own phrasing, outside the Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: allah said, he said. One voice carried inside another, like a letter read aloud. Until next time.

1158.title: I am as My servant thinks
1158.word: I am as My servant thinks
1158.hook: Allah says, I am as My servant thinks of Me (Bukhari)
1158.howItsDone: Muslims may recall this hadith in times of worry or illness, and scholars teach thinking well of Allah as hope joined to prayer, repentance and effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hadith qudsi, a sacred report in which the Prophet relates words from Allah.

Two people get the same voicemail from a doctor's office: please call us back. One spends the afternoon sure it's bad news, rehearsing every outcome. The other assumes it's about rescheduling, and makes lunch. Same message. Two very different afternoons. What a person expects shapes the day they live. Today, one of the sacred hadith, and it's about expecting. Its word is a whole sentence: I am as My servant thinks.
screen: `THE SAME VOICEMAIL.` → `TWO DIFFERENT AFTERNOONS.` → `A SACRED HADITH ABOUT EXPECTING.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ relates that Allah says: I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me. It's short, and it says a great deal. In this report, Allah ties the way He meets a person to what that person expects of Him. Second, the name for it. Scholars call this husn al-zann billah, thinking well of Allah: expecting mercy, forgiveness, an answer. It isn't only for easy days. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet tells his companions that none of them should die except while thinking well of Allah. So this expectation is meant to last to the very end. Third, the balance. Commentators on this hadith add a careful note: thinking well of Allah isn't the same as assuming nothing matters. They pair hope with effort. A person thinks well of Allah while praying, while repenting, while trying. A student who studies and hopes for a good grade is thinking well. A student who skips every class and hopes is only guessing. Fourth, the next lines. The same report goes on: if he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself, and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than it. Remembering runs both ways. After that, the report keeps going, into a picture of distance and of speed. That picture is tomorrow's.
screen: `I AM AS MY SERVANT THINKS OF ME.` · `THINKING WELL OF ALLAH, TO THE END.` · `HOPE THAT WALKS WITH EFFORT.` · `REMEMBERING RUNS BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that's worrying you, hold it gently, and notice what you've been expecting about it, maybe the worst, maybe nothing at all. Without pretending the worry isn't real, try the other way of expecting: if you believe, meet it expecting Allah's mercy; if you're not sure what you believe, simply expect that some good can still come of it. Breathe in on the worry, breathe out on the better expectation, and don't force anything.

1159.title: Draw near a span
1159.hook: whoever draws near Me a span, I draw near a cubit, whoever comes walking, I come running (Bukhari)
1159.howItsDone: Muslims recall this hadith when returning to prayer or repentance after a gap, and teachers use it to encourage small, steady steps rather than waiting to feel ready.

segments.voice: Yesterday: I am as My servant thinks, and thinking well of Allah, with hope and effort together.

Spread your hand wide, thumb to little finger. That's a span, an old way of measuring from before tape measures. Now hold out your forearm, elbow to fingertip. That's a cubit. Now stretch both arms out as far as they go, like you're about to hug someone. That's a fathom. Three measures, all carried on the body. Yesterday's sacred hadith keeps going, and it uses exactly these three. Today: draw near a span.
screen: `A SPAN: THE HAND SPREAD WIDE.` → `A CUBIT: ELBOW TO FINGERTIP.` → `A FATHOM: BOTH ARMS OPEN.`

segments.voice: First, the words. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ relates that Allah says: if My servant draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near a cubit, I draw near a fathom; and if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running. Three measures, each bigger than the last. Second, the arithmetic. Who moves first in the sentence? The servant, and only a little. And the answer is never the same size as the step. It's always more. A span gets a cubit. A cubit gets open arms. Walking gets running. Third, how scholars read the picture. Not all the same way. Some explained the running as the speed of Allah's mercy and help, His answer reaching a person faster and fuller than the effort that reached for Him. Others accepted the words as they come, without asking how, and without likening Allah to anything. Both readings keep the point: the response outruns the step. The Qur'an speaks of the same nearness in its own way, in Pickthall's translation: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." Fourth, a picture from ordinary life. A toddler takes one wobbly step toward a parent across the kitchen. The parent doesn't stand still and wait for the whole distance to be crossed. They come, fast, and scoop the child up. So the smallest step counts. One prayer after a long gap. One honest word of repentance. One kind act. The hadith doesn't ask for a marathon. It asks for a span.
screen: `A SPAN, A CUBIT, A FATHOM.` · `THE ANSWER IS ALWAYS LARGER.` · `TWO WAYS OF READING THE RUNNING.` · `ONE WOBBLY STEP IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Lay your hand flat on your knee, spread wide: a span. Choose one small step within reach today, not a whole new life: if you pray, maybe one prayer you've been missing or a few minutes with the Qur'an; if you don't, maybe a call to someone you've drifted from, or an apology you've been carrying. Then breathe with the hadith's picture: a step taken, and an answer running to meet it.
Draw near a span. The smallest step toward Allah, and in this sacred hadith, an answer that is always larger, coming running. Today's word.
Your line: he comes running. A span is enough to begin. Tomorrow: the hadith of Jibril.

1160.title: The hadith of Jibril
1160.hook: Islam, iman, ihsan, and the signs of the Hour, taught in one scene (Muslim)
1160.howItsDone: Muslims study the hadith of Jibril as a summary of the religion, and teachers use it to introduce Islam, iman and ihsan to new students.

segments.voice: Yesterday: draw near a span, and an answer that always comes larger: he comes running.

Umar ibn al-Khattab tells this one himself. One day, he says, we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, when a man came up to us, his clothes intensely white, his hair intensely black. No mark of travel on him, and not one of us knew him. He sat down close, his knees against the Prophet's knees, his hands on his thighs, and began to ask questions. Long ago on this path we stopped at one of those questions, the one about ihsan. Today, the whole scene. The hadith of Jibril.
screen: `WHITE CLOTHES, BLACK HAIR.` → `KNEES TO KNEES.` → `THE WHOLE SCENE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Three questions first. What is Islam? The Prophet names the pillars: the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage for whoever is able. What is iman, faith? To believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree, its good and its bad. What is ihsan? To worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, He sees you. After each answer the stranger says: you have spoken truly. Umar says they were amazed: a man who asks and then confirms. Second, the question with no date. When is the Hour? And the Prophet answers: the one being asked knows no more about it than the one asking. A teacher, in front of his students, saying I don't know, and making it part of the lesson. Third, the signs. Then tell me its signs, the man says. The Prophet names two. That a slave woman will give birth to her mistress. And that you'll see barefoot, unclothed, destitute shepherds competing in building tall buildings. Commentators have read these in more than one way; several readings point to a world turned upside down. Fourth, the reveal. The man leaves. Umar says he stayed a while, and then the Prophet asked him: Umar, do you know who the questioner was? Allah and His Messenger know best, Umar says. It was Jibril, the Prophet tells him. He came to teach you your religion. So in this report the whole religion arrives as questions, asked by someone who already knew the answers, so the people sitting there could hear them.
screen: `ISLAM, IMAN, IHSAN.` · `THE ONE ASKED KNOWS NO MORE.` · `TWO SIGNS OF THE HOUR.` · `HE CAME TO TEACH YOU YOUR RELIGION.`

segments.voice: Tell the scene back to yourself, one beat per breath: the stranger in white, knees to knees, the three questions, the Hour, the two signs, Umar, do you know who that was? Then let it go quiet, and pick one question to sit with this week: what you do, what you believe, or how you do it.

1161.title: Women who carried hadith
1161.hook: Aisha, and later scholars like Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih
1161.howItsDone: Students of hadith learn the names of women narrators and teachers, from Aisha onward, and some modern scholars have gathered their lives into studies of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hadith of Jibril, and the religion taught as questions: islam, iman, ihsan.

Cover me, cover me. A man has come home from a cave on a mountain, his heart pounding, and those are his words to his wife. It's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, home from Hira, at the beginning of revelation, and the report sits near the start of Sahih al-Bukhari. Who tells it? A woman: Aisha, his wife. Inside her telling, another woman answers him. And much later, a third woman would sit with this very book and teach it. Today, women who carried hadith.
screen: `COVER ME, COVER ME.` → `A WOMAN'S VOICE.` → `ONE BOOK, THREE WOMEN.`

segments.voice: First, Aisha, the narrator, whom you've met before as a scholar in her own right. She tells of the cave, the angel, the command to read, and the Prophet coming home shaken. Her account of the beginning sits on the book's opening pages. She's also the source for reports on how he prayed at night, how he lived at home, what he said in private. Second, Khadijah, inside the story. In Aisha's telling, the Prophet tells Khadijah he fears for himself. And Khadijah answers: never, by Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. Then she says why. You keep ties with your relatives. You carry the burdens of the weak. You help the one who has nothing. You honor your guest. You stand by people in their hardships. Then she takes him to her cousin Waraqah. So the first comfort in this report comes from a woman, and the report itself comes from a woman. Third, Karimah, the teacher. Long after, a scholar named Karimah al-Marwaziyyah taught Bukhari's Sahih in Mecca. Students came to read the book with her, and wrote her into their chains: she narrated it to us. Her name went into the line by which this book was handed on. Fourth, the shape of it. One book, three women. A woman tells the story. Inside it, a woman gives the first comfort. And a woman teaches the book that holds them both. The science this path has followed for weeks asks of every narrator: trustworthy? careful? did they really hear it? Women narrators were asked the same questions. Their names are in the chains because of the answers.

1162.title: Memorizing chains
1162.hook: students memorized chains and texts by heart
1162.howItsDone: Students of hadith traditionally learn reports with their chains from a teacher, and many Muslims memorize short hadith, such as "religion is sincere counsel", as a way of keeping them close.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the women who carried hadith, Aisha, Khadijah and Karimah, and your line: she taught the sahih.

So-and-so told us, from so-and-so, from so-and-so, who heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ say. That's how the lesson begins, in a circle of students on a mosque floor, with no book open. Names first, then the saying. The students hold the names too, in order, because the names are how anyone will later know whether the saying can be trusted. Drop one link and the report limps. Swap two names and a careful critic will notice. Tradition tells of students who kept both, chain and text, in the one place no thief could reach. Today: memorizing chains.
screen: `NO BOOK OPEN.` → `NAMES FIRST, THEN THE SAYING.` → `KEPT WHERE NO THIEF COULD REACH.`

segments.voice: Start with the little word that did the heavy lifting: haddathana, he told us. In the collections it comes link after link, and each one is a person who sat in front of another person. To memorize a chain was to memorize a line of people. Next, why memory, when there was paper? Scholars wrote as well, and their notebooks mattered. But the two checked each other. A student who knew a report by heart could catch a copyist's slip, and a written page could catch a slip of memory. Then the reason underneath it all. In a report preserved by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet asks Allah to make radiant the face of a person who hears a saying from him, holds on to it, and passes it on. In another version, the person passes it on just as he heard it. That phrase sits under the whole enterprise, and it's why a narrator's memory was tested alongside his honesty. Last, a look back, because today closes the week. The four books of the Shia. The sacred hadith, where Allah speaks in the Prophet's phrasing: I am as My servant thinks of Me; whoever comes walking, He comes running. Islam, iman and ihsan, taught in one scene. Women like Karimah, who taught the Sahih. Every one of those reached this lesson because a person held it carefully, often by heart, and handed it on just as it was heard.
screen: `HADDATHANA: HE TOLD US.` · `MEMORY AND PAPER CHECK EACH OTHER.` · `JUST AS HE HEARD IT.` · `A WEEK OF THINGS HELD BY HEART.`

If you pray, you can carry the line into your prayer; if not, just sit with those four words.
